paragraphs.text: A [red tea](red:definition) grown in Taiwan. The label names only [the island](taiwan:on-a-label), not a mountain or township, so it tells you where the leaf grew and nothing finer. Red tea on the island dates from [the Japanese period](red:history), when it was first made at Yuchi near Sun Moon Lake, in the centre of [the island's tea country](taiwan:areas).

It is the fully oxidised tea that English calls black. The fresh leaf is [withered](red:making) until it is soft enough to work, then rolled so its juices and enzymes meet. It is left in warm, damp air until it turns reddish brown, and dried with hot air to end the change and keep it stable.

This lot is from 2023, so it is three years old. Red tea has [no tradition of ageing](red:ageing): sealed, it keeps for about a year and a half to three years, and this tea now sits at the far end of that span.

brewing.text: Red tea takes water near the boil, about 90 to 100°C; hotter water draws out its aroma and flavour more fully, but its bitterness faster too. In a pot or mug, use about a rounded spoon of leaf for each cup and steep three to five minutes, less for broken leaf and a little less, and a little cooler, for a light, delicate tea. Left too long, it turns bitter and drying, because time and heat pull more tannins from the leaf.

notice.text: A sweet cup, often with honey, floral or fruity notes, malt in many, and a brisk strength in the stronger teas. The liquor runs red, bright to deep.
